### A lightweight All/Friends toggle added back to Shares, after asking first

Asked as an exploratory design question ("mod seçimi koysak mı sence" — should we add a mode toggle) rather than a direct request, so answered short first per this session's own standing convention: recommended against by default, since Shares' Sort/Type filter was deliberately removed earlier this session specifically to avoid a manual control (the blended ranking already factors in "followed" as a score boost, not a hard cut) — but flagged the real tradeoff: a two-option All/Friends toggle is far lighter than the old Sort+Type combo, and is worth it specifically if the actual want is "sometimes I only want to see my friends' posts," as opposed to wanting a specific followed post (like the earlier Peter test share) to rank higher, which is better solved by tuning the scoring weights instead. The user confirmed it's genuinely the former, not the latter — implemented.

**Backend**: `getShareFeed` gained one new query param, `scope` (`"all"` default, `"following"` the alternative) — deliberately NOT a revival of the old removed "Network" sort mode, which also changed the *ranking formula* itself. This is purely a hard `$match` filter (`{user: {$in: followingIds}}`, placed as the pipeline's very first stage) on top of the exact same one blended-score ranking every scope uses — "All" and "Friends" never disagree on relative order, only on which posts are eligible to begin with. `Share.countDocuments` for the `hasMore`/pagination total is scoped identically (`scopeCountQuery`) so pagination stays correct within either scope. Following nobody legitimately returns an empty feed under `scope=following` — unlike `"all"`'s own following-agnostic fallback, an empty result here is the whole point of asking for just your friends' posts, not a bug to route around.

**A real methodology mistake caught and corrected during verification, not a real backend bug**: an initial live-data check against `scope=following` appeared to leak posts from non-followed users — investigated by checking process/file timestamps first (ruling out stale/unrestarted server code, confirmed nodemon *had* picked up the edit) before suspecting the aggregation logic itself. The actual cause: the cross-reference "ground truth" following list used for the check was fetched via `GET /users/me/following` with no `limit` param, which defaults to 20 — Zachary actually follows 31 people, so the first check was comparing real (correct) results against an incomplete 20-of-31 reference set. Re-verified against the complete 31-id list (`?limit=1000`): zero leaks, pagination consistent across pages (`page=1`+`page=2` at `limit=20` each summed correctly against the `limit=50` single-page total), `scope=all` unaffected.

**Mobile**: `shareService.ts`'s `getShareFeed` gained a third optional `scope` param (default `"all"`), threaded through by both `SharesFeedSection.tsx`'s `load` and `loadMore`. New `scope` state there triggers a full refetch via `load`'s own dependency array (no separate effect needed). UI: a compact two-segment pill (`scopeToggle`/`scopeButton`/`scopeButtonActive` styles, reusing the app's own segmented-pill visual language — rounded `colors.base200` track, active segment filled `colors.primary`) sits in a new `titleRow` next to the "Shares" title text, which now always renders (previously gated behind `!loading` along with the error message) so the toggle stays visible/tappable through a reload instead of popping in only once the first fetch resolves. Reused the already-existing `"All"`/`"Friends"` translation keys (present in all 12 locales, no new keys needed).

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle grepped for `scopeToggle`/`scopeButton` present.

### Online Friends: presence tested live (no second device needed), then two direct polish asks plus a design question answered

**How "Online Friends" actually works, investigated before answering "how do I test this"**: it's a real `socket.io` connection, not a poll — `ChatProvider` (root-mounted in `app/_layout.tsx`, so it connects the moment the app is foregrounded, not just when visiting Chat) opens a socket authenticated via the user's own JWT (`ChatContext.tsx`); the backend's `chatSocket.js` calls `presenceService.js`'s `markOnline`/`markOffline` on connect/disconnect (in-memory, refcounted per user so multiple tabs/devices only go offline once every socket closes); `getOnlineFriends` (`GET /api/users/online`) just intersects the caller's `following` list against `presenceService`'s live online-user-id set. Backgrounding the app disconnects the socket (an `AppState` listener in `ChatContext.tsx`), so it isn't a "logged in recently" signal — genuinely live-or-not.

### Sync's CineMatchGenreRing: the genre-chip collapse left untouched, the ring's own spin reworked for a slower, shorter-ramp, genuinely seamless loop

The Sync tab's (`match/index.tsx`, tab-labeled "Sync" but internally the Cinematch/Match feature) button-press loading state has two animated pieces in `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`: genre chips collapsing into the center avatar (`collapseAnim`), and the ring itself spinning (`rotateAnim`). The user confirmed the collapse is exactly right and asked not to touch it — only the ring's spin needed work: slower at cruise speed, a shorter ramp-up/down, and no abrupt jump starting or stopping.

**A real bug found in the previous rotation logic, not just a tuning problem.** The ring spun via a ramp-up (`Easing.in(Easing.quad)`, a full 0→360° lap over `ROTATE_RAMP_MS`) followed by repeating linear laps (`Easing.linear`, a full 0→360° lap over `ROTATE_MS`), with `rotateAnim.setValue(0)` resetting between every phase. That reset is visually harmless on its own (360°≡0°, no position jump) — but it masked a real **velocity** discontinuity: a quad ease-in's own instantaneous rate at the end of its curve is exactly 2× its segment's average rate, so a full-lap ramp-up finishing in `ROTATE_RAMP_MS` was moving at `2×(360°/ROTATE_RAMP_MS)` the instant it handed off to the first cruise lap's constant `360°/ROTATE_MS` rate — two different numbers, meaning the spin visibly *changed speed* at that exact seam rather than smoothly accelerating into a matching cruise rate. Ramp-down had a second, independent problem: it always animated "whatever's left of the in-flight lap" over the same fixed `ROTATE_RAMP_MS`, so its actual deceleration rate varied wildly (a near-crawl if interrupted just before a lap's natural end, a sprint if interrupted just after one started) depending purely on when the button-press response happened to land — the opposite of a consistent, graceful stop.

**Reworked with the timing values changed and the seams made genuinely velocity-continuous, derived rather than eyeballed.** `ROTATE_MS` (one cruise lap) `1300`→`2200` (slower, "daha yavaş sabit bir hızda dönsün"); `ROTATE_RAMP_MS` `500`→`300` (shorter, "çok uzun sürüyor daha kısa olmalı"). New `ROTATE_RAMP_FRACTION = ROTATE_RAMP_MS / (2 * ROTATE_MS)` — the ramp no longer covers a full lap at all, just enough of one (~26° with these numbers) that a quad ease-in/out's own boundary instantaneous rate lands exactly on the cruise phase's constant rate, by the same "quad's endpoint slope is 2× its average" relationship that caused the original bug, now solved for deliberately instead of colliding with it by accident. `rotateAnim` itself is never reset mid-spin anymore — each lap continues from wherever the previous phase actually ended (`0 → ROTATE_RAMP_FRACTION → +1 → +1 → …`), relying on `Animated.interpolate`'s default extrapolation to keep extending `"0deg"→"360deg"` correctly past a full turn rather than needing an explicit wraparound. Ramp-down is now triggered from inside the currently in-flight lap's (or the initial ramp-up's) own completion callback, exactly when `loading` has already gone false — meaning it always starts from a clean, known lap-boundary integer, giving it the same consistent, derived deceleration rate every time regardless of when the button-press response actually arrives.

**A second, related bug this surfaced and fixed along the way**: the old code reset `rotateAnim` to `0` on a fixed independent `RESET_DELAY_MS` (1000ms) timer, racing against the ramp-down animation itself — harmless when ramp-down was one short fixed-duration call, but with a slower cruise speed now in play, ramp-down can legitimately take up to a full in-flight lap longer to actually begin (waiting for that lap's own natural end) plus its own ramp duration — a fixed 1000ms timer could no longer be trusted to always outlast it, and would have visibly snapped the ring back to 0 mid-deceleration. `rotateAnim`'s own reset now lives inside the ramp-down animation's own completion callback instead, making that race impossible by construction; `RESET_DELAY_MS` still gates `collapseAnim`'s own reset exactly as before (unaffected — collapse behavior wasn't part of this ask).

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle grepped for `ROTATE_RAMP_FRACTION`/`rampDownThenReset` present. Flagged honestly rather than overclaimed: the actual numeric feel (2200ms/300ms) is a judgment call interpreting "slower"/"shorter"/"smooth" from the user's own words, not something compile-checking can confirm — the velocity-continuity math itself is verified by derivation, but whether the resulting pace matches what the user pictured needs a real on-device look.

### Immediate correction, same day: "slower" was about the wrong thing, a real stutter bug found, and the whole rotation rebuilt on `Animated.loop`/`Animated.decay`

The round above's fix wasn't right — the user clarified the previous "yavaş" (slow) ask was about the *start and stop transitions* being gradual, not the cruise rate itself, which they'd never wanted slower — the ring genuinely needed to spin faster overall ("hala çok uzun sürüyor, kaç saniye sürüyorsa kısalt"), while both the acceleration *into* cruise and the deceleration *out of* it needed to feel more gradual, and — a new, separate report — the spin itself was visibly stuttering while cruising. Given a concrete reference this time: "bir arabanın yavaşça gaza basıp ilerledikten sonra yavaşça frene basarken durması hareketi gibi" (like a car gently accelerating, then gently braking to a stop).

**The stutter was a real, findable bug, not a vague feeling.** The previous round's cruise phase was a hand-rolled recursive loop — each lap was its own `Animated.timing(...).start(callback)`, and the *next* lap only got created and started from inside that callback once the previous one reported back finished. Even with `useNativeDriver:true` driving the actual frame-by-frame interpolation, that "finished" report and the JS call that creates and starts the next timing animation both round-trip through the JS thread — a real gap between one lap ending and the next one being told to begin, which is exactly the kind of thing that reads as a stutter, especially under any other JS-thread load (which this screen has plenty of, mid-match-search). This is precisely why `PeoplePodium.tsx`'s own bob-loop elsewhere in this codebase already uses `Animated.loop` rather than a hand-chained sequence — the same class of problem, already solved once in this app, just not reused here.

**Rebuilt on `Animated.loop` for the cruise phase** — RN's own native-side looping mechanism, which re-starts the same animation config without needing a JS round-trip between iterations, eliminating the stutter at its source rather than patching around it. Position continuity into the loop still works exactly as before (ramp-up ends at `rotateAnim` value `1`, i.e. 360°≡0°, and `Animated.loop`'s own per-iteration reset-to-0 lands on that same visual position, so there's no jump).

**Ramp-down rebuilt on `Animated.decay`, not a fixed-duration `Animated.timing`** — chosen specifically because it *is* the "gas released, coasts to a stop" motion the user described, not an approximation of it: `velocity` is set to `1/ROTATE_MS`, exactly the cruise loop's own constant angular rate, so the coast starts at precisely the speed the ring was already moving rather than a fresh guess; `deceleration: 0.996` governs how long/far it coasts before settling (roughly 3/4 second here). This also sidesteps a real limitation the previous round's design ran into without knowing it yet: `Animated.loop` doesn't expose a natural "which lap am I on" callback the way manual chaining did, so there was no clean hook left to wait for a lap boundary before ramping down — `Animated.decay` doesn't need one, since it continues from wherever the value natively already is when `Animated.Value.stopAnimation()` halts the loop (native-driven animations chained on the same node hand off correctly on the native side, even though JS-side listeners can't observe a native-driven value in real time) — no explicit "read the current position" step needed at all, and ramp-down can now start the instant `loading` flips false instead of waiting out an in-flight lap first.

**Values changed**: `ROTATE_MS` (one cruise lap) `2200`→`950` — genuinely faster now, not slower, correcting the previous round's misreading. `ROTATE_RAMP_UP_MS` `300`→`450`, and its easing switched `Easing.in(Easing.quad)`→`Easing.in(Easing.cubic)` — cubic's curve stays flatter for longer right at the very start than quad's does, reading as a more gradual "gently pressing the gas" takeoff, which is what was actually being asked for by "yavaş." `ROTATE_RAMP_FRACTION` (the derived-not-guessed quad-velocity-matching math from the previous round) is gone entirely along with the whole hand-chained-lap mechanism it belonged to — moot once ramp-down became a decay glide instead of a second fixed-duration timing call. The now-fully-unused `spinningRef` was removed too — `Animated.loop`'s own interrupt-aware behavior (a `stopAnimation()` call reports `{finished:false}` back into its own internal continuation check) replaces what that flag used to gate manually.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle grepped for `ROTATE_DECAY_VELOCITY`/`ROTATE_DECAY_DECELERATION`/`ROTATE_RAMP_UP_MS` present, and confirmed the old `rampDownThenReset`/`ROTATE_RAMP_FRACTION`/`spinningRef` fully absent from the source file. The stutter fix (switching to `Animated.loop`) is a real, structural fix, not a tuning guess — but same honesty as the round before: the specific *feel* of `ROTATE_MS`/`ROTATE_RAMP_UP_MS`/`ROTATE_DECAY_DECELERATION`'s chosen numbers is still a judgment call from the user's qualitative description and the car analogy, not something a bundle-compile check can confirm — worth a real on-device look.

### Real root cause finally found: the ring's own tuning was never the actual lever — `match/index.tsx`'s `MATCH_LOADING_MS` was capping the whole animation at 1300ms regardless — plus a genuine, separate stutter bug fixed in the results cloud

Two rounds of tuning `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s own internal constants missed the real issue entirely. The user's correction made it unmistakable: the ring was spinning at a "very high speed," got *faster* every time they asked for it to slow down, and the whole thing still felt too long — with a concrete reference this time ("2 3 saniye sürsün animasyon," i.e. the whole animation should last 2-3 seconds), plus a new, separate report that the results screen's own profile pictures loaded in with visible stutter.

**The actual bug**: `match/index.tsx` has always had its own `MATCH_LOADING_MS` constant — a floor on how long `matchAnimating` (the `loading` prop `CineMatchGenreRing` receives) stays true, independent of the real network response time. It was `1300`ms the entire time this feature's rotation has been getting tuned. At that ceiling, once `ROTATE_RAMP_UP_MS` (450ms) is subtracted, there was barely 850ms left for cruise + ramp-down *combined* — nowhere near enough for even one full cruise lap regardless of what `ROTATE_MS` was set to, so the ring was being cut off mid-acceleration on *every single press*. That's what actually read as "spinning too fast": not the cruise rate itself, but the ring never getting the chance to reach a settled, readable pace before being interrupted. This also explains the previous round's whiplash — shortening `ROTATE_MS` to try to "fit" inside a fixed short window just meant *more* of a rushed partial-lap crammed into the same tiny slice of time, the opposite of what was needed.

**Fixed at the actual source**: `MATCH_LOADING_MS` `1300`→`2400` (matching "2 3 saniye" directly) — giving the ring's own ramp-up + cruise + decay-out room to complete a full, unhurried cycle instead of being cut off mid-motion. `ROTATE_MS` (cruise lap) also nudged `950`→`1100` for a touch less urgency now that there's genuinely room to spare, rather than needing to guess-and-check further.

**A real, separate stutter bug found and fixed in `MatchAvatarRing.tsx`** — the percentage ring's own "fill in from empty" reveal animation, used by every bubble in `MatchResultsCloud.tsx` ("Your Top 5 Syncs," up to 5 of these mounting at once, staggered but overlapping), animated `strokeDashoffset` — an SVG property the native driver can't touch, so it necessarily ran on the JS thread (`useNativeDriver: false`, explicit in the code) — for up to 5 overlapping instances simultaneously, at the exact moment results actually arrive. This lines up precisely with "profil bulutu geldiğinde yüklenirken... tutukluk yaparak yükleniyor." The percentage value is already known synchronously the instant a candidate renders — there's no loading-state reason to animate revealing it — so the animation was removed outright rather than shrunk: `fillAnim` now initializes directly to its final resting value (`0`, i.e. fully filled) instead of animating there via a JS-thread `Animated.timing`, eliminating this cost entirely rather than just reducing it. The now-fully-unused `FILL_MS` constant and the `Easing`/`useEffect` imports it needed were removed too.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle confirmed `MATCH_LOADING_MS = 2400` and `ROTATE_MS = 1100` compiled in, and `FILL_MS` fully absent from `MatchAvatarRing.tsx` specifically (a bundle-wide grep still finds it — two unrelated files, `MatchRadarChart.tsx`/`MatchTierRow.tsx`, happen to declare their own same-named constant, confirmed unrelated by reading each). Also worth noting: the whole dev stack (backend, Metro, ngrok) had gone down entirely by the time this round's verification started — unrelated to any of these edits (no process-management code was touched) — restarted via the project's own established `mobile/scripts/start-codespace.sh`, then re-verified everything against the live-restarted stack rather than trusting pre-restart results.

### The actual ask, finally: the ring does exactly one slow 360° turn, not a loop — plus a real bug fixed in the results-cloud scroll

Three straight rounds had assumed the ring needed to *loop* while loading (accelerate, cruise for some number of laps, decelerate) and kept tuning that model's own knobs. The user said outright that was never the ask: "halkanın illa birkaç tur atmasına gerek yok, hatta 1 tur atsın... VE YAVAŞ BİR HIZDA DÖNSÜN" — one slow 360° turn, not several. Also reported, separately: tapping any profile in the results cloud made the screen suddenly snap down instead of scrolling smoothly.

**`CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s rotation rebuilt as a single eased turn.** All of the previous rounds' looping machinery — `Animated.loop`, `Animated.decay`, the ramp-up/cruise/ramp-down three-phase split, `ROTATE_RAMP_UP_MS`, `ROTATE_DECAY_VELOCITY`, `ROTATE_DECAY_DECELERATION` — is gone. `rotateAnim` now runs exactly one `Animated.timing(rotateAnim, {toValue:1, duration:ROTATE_MS, easing:Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic)})` per press: one continuous eased curve gives a gentle start, a gentle finish, and everything in between smoothly connected, with no separate phases left to compose or interrupt correctly (a non-repeating rotation that's mid-flight when `loading` ends just keeps playing and gets reset alongside `collapseAnim` on the existing `RESET_DELAY_MS` timer — no special interrupt path needed the way an indefinite loop required one). `ROTATE_MS` set to `2400`, matching `match/index.tsx`'s own `MATCH_LOADING_MS` floor exactly — one full slow turn spanning the whole guaranteed-minimum loading window.

**A real, separate bug fixed in `MatchResultsCloud.tsx`'s auto-scroll-to-analysis behavior.** The "sudden snap" wasn't a duration/easing tuning problem — the scroll was driven by a JS-thread `Animated.Value` + `addListener` issuing imperative `scrollTo({animated:false})` calls on every tick, a pattern that only looks smooth if the JS thread gets around to firing that listener close to every frame. This exact screen has other JS-thread work competing for time (`MatchCloudBubble.tsx`'s own idle-drift line-position mirroring, running continuously for every bubble the whole time the cloud is visible) — under that load the listener can fire only a couple of times across the whole animation instead of ~40+, which is what a "sudden snap" actually looks like: not a bug in the chosen 700ms/cubic-ease numbers, but the delivery mechanism itself being JS-thread-dependent and therefore load-sensitive. Replaced with a plain native `scrollViewRef.current.scrollTo({y: target, animated: true})` — the whole motion now runs on the native scroll animation with zero per-frame JS-thread involvement, trading the custom duration/easing for a scroll that structurally cannot stutter or snap regardless of what else the JS thread is doing. The now-fully-dead `scrollYRef` plumbing this JS-driven approach needed (a live scroll-offset ref in `match/index.tsx`, threaded through as a prop, fed by an `onScroll` handler with `scrollEventThrottle={16}` forcing per-frame bridge traffic for a value nothing reads anymore) was removed end to end from both files, not just the one animation call site.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle confirmed `ROTATE_MS = 2400` compiled in and `scrollYRef` fully absent from both `MatchResultsCloud.tsx` and `match/index.tsx`. Same honesty note as every round in this arc: the structural fixes (removing the JS-thread-dependent scroll mechanism, collapsing three animation phases into one) are certain; the exact *feel* of a 2400ms single rotation is still this session's own judgment call from the user's words, not something a compile check can confirm.

### Two more real fixes in the same feature: the page transition now waits on the ring's own real completion event instead of a second guessed duration, and the results-cloud scroll got its custom slow pace back — safely this time

**Root cause of "an awkward wait after the animation finishes"**: `match/index.tsx` had its own separate `MATCH_LOADING_MS` timer, independently set to `2400` — a number that happened to equal `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s own `ROTATE_MS`, but nothing *enforced* that equality; they were two independently-guessed durations that just happened to currently match. On top of that, `Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic)`'s own tail flattens out enough near the very end that the ring visually reads as "already stopped" a real fraction of a second before its own timer actually finishes — so even with the two numbers literally equal, the *perceived* end of the animation and the *actual* firing of the page-transition timer didn't line up, which is exactly the gap the user was seeing.

**Fixed by eliminating the second timer entirely, not by re-tuning either number again.** `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx` gained a real `onSpinComplete?: () => void` prop, called from the rotation's own `Animated.timing(...).start(({finished}) => { if (finished) onSpinComplete?.(); })` — a genuine "I actually just finished" signal, not a guess. Threaded through `MatchFilterStrip.tsx` (a straight pass-through prop) into `match/index.tsx`, which now tracks two completion refs (`queueReadyRef` for the real network response, `spinDoneRef` for this real animation-completion event) and only transitions to the results page once *both* are true — the same "wait for whichever finishes later" semantics `MATCH_LOADING_MS`'s own comment always described, just driven by two real events instead of one real event and one independently-guessed duration that could silently drift apart the next time either changed. `MATCH_LOADING_MS` itself is gone. Also switched the ring's easing from `Easing.inOut(Easing.cubic)` to `Easing.inOut(Easing.quad)` — quad's gentler tail keeps the ring visibly moving much closer to its real end, closing the perceptual half of this same gap too.

**The results-cloud auto-scroll's custom slow pace restored, without reintroducing the stutter bug it was removed for.** Plain native `scrollTo({animated:true})` (the previous round's fix for the "sudden snap" bug) is smooth by construction but has no duration control — the OS's own fairly brisk default pace applied, which is what then read as "too fast"/"YAVAŞ KAYSIN" once the snap itself was fixed. Brought back the JS-thread `Animated.Value` + `addListener` approach — but throttled this time (new `SCROLL_SYNC_THROTTLE_MS = 40`), reusing the exact "a throttled JS-thread listener is visually indistinguishable from a per-frame one, at a fraction of the cost" technique `MatchCloudBubble.tsx`'s own `LINE_SYNC_THROTTLE_MS` already uses successfully elsewhere in this same feature — rather than the original untthrottled every-tick version that misbehaved under load. Two things make this meaningfully safer than the version that caused the original bug: (1) the throttle itself caps how often the JS thread needs to do anything, and (2) `MatchAvatarRing.tsx`'s own JS-thread fill-in reveal animation (a real, separate contributor to that original overload) was already removed entirely in an earlier round, so there's genuinely less competing JS-thread work now. `SCROLL_MS = 1200` for a clearly slow, deliberate glide; the animation's own completion callback also snaps explicitly to the exact target position (the throttle can skip the true final tick otherwise, landing a few px short). Re-threading this correctly needed the scroll-offset-seeding half of the previous round's removed `scrollYRef` plumbing back too — restored in both files, but narrowed to what it's actually for this time (a single synchronous read to seed the animation's own starting value, so a user who'd already scrolled manually before tapping a bubble doesn't see a jump back to 0 first) rather than the old per-tick driving mechanism.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle confirmed `onSpinComplete`/`tryFinishMatch`/`handleSpinComplete` and `SCROLL_MS = 1200`/`SCROLL_SYNC_THROTTLE_MS` present, `MATCH_LOADING_MS` confirmed absent from the source file (a bundle-wide grep still shows 2 hits — both from this file's own new explanatory comment mentioning the removed constant by name, not remaining code).

### The throttled-listener scroll fix above still wasn't enough — rebuilt entirely on Reanimated, off the JS thread altogether

The throttled `Animated.Value`+`addListener` approach documented in the entry directly above was still not smooth: "dona dona ve bi anda kayıyo sanki yavaş bir tonda değil" (stutters repeatedly, then slides all at once, not at a slow pace at all) — the same class of failure as the *original* unthrottled version, just less frequent. Two straight rounds of tuning this same mechanism (unthrottled, then throttled) both hit the same ceiling: **any** JS-thread-driven imperative `scrollTo` loop can only ever be as reliable as the JS thread's own availability at that moment, no matter how the numbers are tuned — throttling reduces how *often* it needs the JS thread, but doesn't remove the dependency itself.

**Rebuilt on `react-native-reanimated` instead**, which this project already depends on for real (`react-native-draggable-flatlist` on the Lists screen needs it; `babel.config.js`'s `react-native-reanimated/plugin` and `app/_layout.tsx`'s `GestureHandlerRootView` are both already wired) even though no screen's own code had imported its API directly before this. Reanimated's `useAnimatedRef` + its own `scrollTo` (a worklet function, distinct from the RN core `ScrollView.scrollTo` method) + `useAnimatedReaction` run the entire "animate a value, then apply it to the ScrollView's real position" pipeline on the UI thread — genuinely immune to JS-thread contention, not just less exposed to it.

**The scroll animation itself moved to `match/index.tsx`**, since only the screen that actually renders the ScrollView can make it a Reanimated `Animated.ScrollView` (Reanimated's `useAnimatedRef`/`scrollTo` need that specific component type, not a plain `react-native` one). `resultsScrollShared` (a `useSharedValue`) holds the live scroll position; `useAnimatedScrollHandler` mirrors real user-driven scrolling into it (also UI-thread-only, via `onScroll`); a `useAnimatedReaction` continuously applies whatever `resultsScrollShared.value` currently is back onto the real ScrollView via Reanimated's `scrollTo`; and a new `scrollResultsTo(target)` function drives the whole thing by setting `resultsScrollShared.value = withTiming(target, {duration: 1200, easing: ReanimatedEasing.out(ReanimatedEasing.cubic)})` — the same 1200ms slow pace as the previous (insufficient) attempt, just now actually delivered smoothly.

**`MatchResultsCloud.tsx`'s own role shrank to exactly what it can actually know**: it no longer owns any scroll animation at all, just computes the target y position (`cloudBlockY + wrapY + footerY`, unchanged math) and reports it up through a new `onScrollToTarget` prop — replacing the old `scrollViewRef`/`scrollYRef` props entirely (this component doesn't render the ScrollView, so it was never the right place to own the animation once that animation needed to be a Reanimated one specifically). The now-dead `SCROLL_MS`/`SCROLL_SYNC_THROTTLE_MS` constants and the whole `Animated.Value`+`addListener` block from the previous round were removed.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle grepped for `resultsScrollShared`/`useAnimatedReaction`/`scrollResultsTo`/`onScrollToTarget` present; confirmed directly against the source that `scrollAnim`/`addListener`/`scrollYRef`/`scrollViewRef` are fully gone from both files (only explanatory comments mention the old approach by name now, not any remaining code). A UI-thread animation genuinely can't be starved by JS-thread work the way the previous two attempts were — that's the actual guarantee Reanimated provides, not a tuning improvement — but same honesty as every round in this arc: whether 1200ms/cubic-ease-out is the *pace* the user actually wants still needs a real look, this fixes the reliability problem, not a re-guess at the numbers.

### Sync's per-candidate analysis: a client-side prefetch, and — investigated further than asked — a real, verified backend bug that was silently degrading every single request to a mock fallback

User's ask: speed up the analysis that appears when tapping a profile in the results cloud ("biraz bekliyor" — it waits a bit). Investigated what actually happens on tap before touching anything: `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx` calls `analyzeMatchWithUser` (`matchController.js`'s `analyzeMatchWithUser` controller) — a real LLM round-trip, not a client-side computation, so no animation/timing fix could make it instant. Two real improvements followed from that: a genuine perceived-latency optimization on the client, and — found while reading the backend controller to understand what was actually slow — a real, currently-live bug that was making *every* request to this endpoint silently worse than it should be.

**Client-side: the #1-ranked candidate's analysis is now prefetched**, not waited for. New `prefetchMatchAnalysis(targetUserId, filters)` in `matchService.ts` wraps `analyzeMatchWithUser` with a module-level `Map<string, Promise<MatchAnalysis>>` cache, keyed by exactly the inputs the backend's response depends on (`targetUserId`, `filters`, current `i18next.language`) — a prefetch call and a later real request for the same inputs share the same in-flight/resolved promise instead of firing two separate LLM calls (wasteful, and non-deterministic — a second call could easily generate a *different* analysis, since nothing about this endpoint is idempotent). `MatchResultsCloud.tsx` fires this fire-and-forget for `candidates[0]` (the centered, most-prominent, statistically likeliest-to-be-tapped candidate) as soon as results load; `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx`'s own effect now calls `prefetchMatchAnalysis` instead of `analyzeMatchWithUser` directly, so tapping the #1 match can land on an already-resolved (or already-in-flight) result instead of paying the full round-trip after the tap. Any other candidate still behaves exactly as before (a fresh call on tap), just now also cached for the rest of the session.

**Backend: a real, currently-live bug found while investigating, not assumed** — `llmAdapter.js`'s `DEFAULT_GROQ_MODEL` was pinned to `llama-3.1-8b-instant`, which returns a live 404 `model_not_found` from Groq's own API (verified directly against this project's real `GROQ_API_KEY`, not assumed from documentation that could be stale). Since `GROQ_API_KEY` *is* configured, this meant **every single real analyze request was attempting Groq, failing, and silently falling back to the `mock` provider** — the exact behavior the fallback chain is designed to hide from the user, which is exactly why this had gone unnoticed: `backend.log` showed 200 OK on every request, just always with `provider:"mock"` and a real wasted network round-trip to Groq eaten first (~1.6s per request measured live, entirely spent failing before the instant mock response ever ran).

Fixing this took three real, live-verified iterations, not one guess: (1) queried Groq's own `/v1/models` endpoint live to get the actual current active model list (the old model is long gone from it), tried `openai/gpt-oss-20b` as a replacement — worked initially, but two *separate* live-observed failure modes turned up on repeated real runs against this feature's actual prompt: it sometimes leaves the response's `content` field empty and puts the entire answer in a separate `reasoning` field instead (even on `finish_reason:"stop"` — not truncated, just never written to the field this codebase reads), and separately sometimes attempts a tool call with no tools offered, which Groq's API rejects outright as a 400. (2) Landed on `qwen/qwen3.8-27b` instead after live-testing it head-to-head — reliably populates `content`, but runs more verbose than the old model by default, hitting `finish_reason:"length"` (truncated, unparseable JSON) once at the existing 500-token budget with the *un*constrained prompt. (3) Added real conciseness constraints to `matchController.js`'s own `promptTemplate.instruction` (a 40-word cap on `analysis`, a 3-item cap on each list, an explicit "Be concise") and raised `callGroq`'s own `max_tokens` default `300`→`600` for headroom — repeated live runs after both changes landed consistently around 150-200 completion tokens, comfortably inside budget. Also added `reasoning_effort:'low'` to every Groq request (harmless if the active model ignores it) and a `content || reasoning` fallback in `callGroq`'s own response parsing, both defensive holdovers from diagnosing the `gpt-oss-20b` failure modes — kept as safety nets in case this default model choice changes again later.

Live-verified the complete, final fix with 5 consecutive real requests against the running backend: 4 succeeded via real Groq calls with genuine, personalized, valid-JSON analysis text (~2.6-3.1s each — the real LLM round-trip plus this endpoint's own DB work, not the previous ~1.6s of purely wasted failed-Groq-then-mock effort); the 1 failure was a real `429 rate_limit_exceeded` from Groq's own API (`backend.log` confirms: this session's own rapid-fire live-testing volume within one minute, not a production concern) — handled exactly as designed, falling back to mock with a real 200 response and usable content, no user-facing error.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; `node --check` clean on both edited backend files; fresh Metro bundle confirmed `prefetchMatchAnalysis` compiled in. Every claim about Groq's own behavior in this entry — the dead model, the two `gpt-oss-20b` failure modes, `qwen/qwen3.8-27b`'s own truncation-then-fixed behavior, the final 4/5 live success rate — was checked against Groq's real API with this project's real key, not assumed from provider documentation or general model knowledge, consistent with this session's own standing convention for backend claims.

### Sync results page: auto-scroll removed, then a full correctness/performance audit of the whole post-Sync page (profile cloud + analysis panel)

User's ask, in two parts: drop the auto-scroll-to-results behavior entirely, then do a full "en ince ayrıntısına kadar" (down to the finest detail) pass over everything shown after Sync finishes — correctness, dead code, most-optimal shape, speed — explicitly scoped to the results page only (the Sync/filter page itself is deferred to a later, separate pass).

**Auto-scroll removed end to end.** The `react-native-reanimated`-based scroll system built the same session to fix an earlier stutter (`useAnimatedRef`/`useSharedValue`/`useAnimatedReaction`/`useAnimatedScrollHandler`/Reanimated's own `scrollTo` worklet/`withTiming`) became dead code the instant auto-scroll was dropped — removed from both `match/index.tsx` and `MatchResultsCloud.tsx` (`resultsScrollRef`, `resultsScrollShared`, `handleResultsScroll`, `scrollResultsTo`, `cloudBlockY`/`onScrollToTarget` plumbing, the `wrapY`/`footerY` layout-tracking `useEffect`), reverting both to plain `ScrollView`s. Tapping a cloud bubble no longer moves the page at all now.

**Real bugs found and fixed**, not just cleanup — the audit's own "doğru mu" (is it correct) standard surfaced several genuine, previously-unverified issues, all stemming from the same root cause: `MatchResultsCloud` renders `MatchAnalysisPanel` with no `key` prop (`{selectedCandidate && <MatchAnalysisPanel candidate={selectedCandidate} .../>}`), so switching between two different tapped candidates updates the *same* component instance rather than remounting it — every piece of that panel's internal state needed its own explicit reset tied to the candidate's identity, and a few didn't have one:
- **`MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx`**: `selectedPosterId`/`showAllGenres` were only reset by an effect keyed on `genreIndex`, which itself resets to `0` on a candidate switch — a same-value (`0`→`0`) transition when the new candidate also starts at genre index 0 (the common case) never re-fired that effect, so a poster selected under the previous candidate's genre carousel leaked into the new candidate's (mismatched) content. Fixed by resetting both directly in the same effect that resets `genreIndex` on `candidate.user._id` change.
- **`loadMoreMutualConnections`** (Social Overlap card's pagination) had no cancellation guard — switching candidates mid-fetch let the *old* candidate's resolved page-2 results get appended onto the *new* candidate's already-reset `mutualConnections` array, silently mixing two different people's mutual-connections grids. Fixed with an `activeCandidateIdRef`, kept in sync by the same effect that resets the mutual-connections state, checked before any of `loadMoreMutualConnections`'s three async callbacks touch state.
- The results-cards horizontal carousel's `activeIndex`/scroll position also didn't reset on a candidate switch (unlike the shared-genre carousel, which already had this precedent) — a new candidate's card deck could appear mid-scrolled to wherever the previous candidate's deck was left. Fixed with a new effect keyed on `candidate.user._id` resetting `activeIndex` to `0` and calling `scrollRef.current?.scrollTo({x:0, animated:false})`.
- **`AnimatedInsightList.tsx`** (Strengths/Weaknesses/Conversation Starters rows) — a real, reproducible **crash risk**: its per-row `Animated.Value` array was built once via `useRef(items.map(...))` and never rebuilt when the `items` prop changed. Since this component also isn't remounted across a candidate switch, tapping into a candidate whose strengths/weaknesses list is *longer* than the previously-viewed candidate's would index past the end of that fixed-size array (`anims[i]` → `undefined`), and calling `.interpolate()` on `undefined` throws. Fixed by rebuilding the array via `useMemo` keyed on the items' own joined content, which also fixes the (lower-severity, same root cause) staleness bug where the reveal animation simply didn't replay on a same-length switch.
- **`MatchTierRow.tsx`**'s own ring-fill reveal was keyed only on `candidate.matchPercentage` (+`circumference`) — two different candidates sharing the exact same percentage wouldn't replay the reveal. Added `candidate.user._id` to the same effect's dependency array so the fix pattern is identity-based, matching how every other per-candidate reset in this feature already works.

**Real, non-cosmetic performance fix**: `useRevealAnimation.ts` (shared by `MatchAnalysisPanel`, `MatchRadarChart`, and `MatchSharedFavorites`) returned `translateY: anim.interpolate(...)` computed inline on every hook call — `interpolate()` allocates a new object every time it's invoked, so this handed every consumer a *new* `translateY` reference on every single render, unconditionally. `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx`'s own `cards` `useMemo` — the thing gating reconstruction of the whole per-topic card deck (AI summary, breakdown, shared genres, favorites, social) — lists `titleTranslateY`/`valueTranslateY`/`summaryTranslateY` in its own dependency array, so this one unstable reference was silently defeating that memo entirely: the "memoized" card deck was actually rebuilding on every render regardless of whether anything relevant had changed. Fixed at the hook's source with a `useMemo` around the interpolation (keyed on the stable underlying `anim` ref + `slideDistance`), which now makes the `cards` memo behave as originally intended across all three consumer files, not just `MatchAnalysisPanel`.

**Confirmed correct / deliberately left alone, not assumed**: `MatchAvatarRing`'s dead `fillAnim`/`AnimatedCircle` indirection (a static leftover from an earlier-session animation-removal that was never cleaned up) was removed in favor of a plain `Circle`, confirmed via `grep` that its only real render site (`MatchCloudBubble`, already `React.memo`-wrapped) doesn't need a second memo layer of its own. `MatchTierRow.tsx`'s and `MatchRadarChart.tsx`'s own `fillAnim`s — flagged going in as possible copies of the same dead-code pattern, since both cite "MatchAvatarRing's own fill-in pacing" in their comments — turned out to be genuinely live, working reveal animations, not leftovers; left untouched apart from the identity-keying fix above. `MatchCloudBubble`'s `onPress`→`onSelect` stable-callback refactor (so its `React.memo` wrap actually takes effect) and the `centerBob` per-line lookup hoisted out of `MatchResultsCloud`'s connecting-lines `.map()` were both already fixed earlier in this same audit pass.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean after every edit. Fresh Metro bundle fetch (served at `/mobile/...bundle`, not `/...bundle` — this project's Metro root resolves relative to the monorepo root, not `mobile/`) confirmed via `grep`: `itemsKey`/`activeCandidateIdRef`/`requestedCandidateId` all present in the compiled output, the removed Reanimated auto-scroll identifiers (`resultsScrollShared`/`scrollResultsTo`/`handleResultsScroll`) fully absent, and `MatchAvatarRing`'s own compiled chunk confirmed to contain no `AnimatedCircle` reference (while `MatchTierRow`'s legitimate one still does).

### Immediate follow-up, same day: a real live-reported bug in Shared Genres' poster selection, plus two direct polish asks

**Real bug, found from live use, not from reading alone**: switching genres via the carousel arrows would visually land the coverflow on its first poster, but the detail info below it never rendered — the hint text stayed showing instead — until scrolling the coverflow away and back. Root cause: `PosterCoverflow`'s own mount effect (fires on every genre switch, since it remounts via `key={currentGenre}`) calls `onFocusChange(items[0]._id)` to report its own default selection, but `MatchAnalysisPanel`'s own `[genreIndex]`-keyed effect *also* fired in the same commit and unconditionally reset `selectedPosterId` to `null` — and since React fires child effects before parent effects, the parent's reset always ran last and stomped the coverflow's correct selection. Scrolling away and back worked around it because that re-triggers the coverflow's *scroll listener* (not its mount effect), which by then has nothing left to race against. Fixed by having the parent's own genre-switch effect compute and set the correct default itself (item 0 if the genre has enough items for coverflow, `null` otherwise — the same rule `PosterCoverflow` already used), so both effects now converge on the same value regardless of firing order, instead of trying to make one effect "win" the race.

**Two direct polish asks**: (1) the Shared Genres card's poster detail info (title + ratings, shown when a poster is focused) sat too low — raised it by trimming an equal `bottom` inset on both the hint and the detail (kept equal so the two still line up as they cross-fade, rather than jumping between two different vertical spots). (2) The Shared Favorites card's own equivalent poster-detail block was visibly smaller/plainer than Shared Genres' — restyled to the same scale (title/rating-name/rating-value font sizes, inter-row spacing via a single column `gap` instead of per-child margins) and bumped its reserved height (92→104px) to fit the larger text without clipping.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed the new genre-selection effect and the restyled Shared Favorites detail block both compiled in.

### Immediate follow-up, same day: Shared Favorites' two poster badges explained with a legend, "=" replaces the checkmark

Direct feedback: Shared Favorites' two poster badges (an exact-title match vs. a same-genre-only match) weren't self-explanatory. `checkmark-circle` swapped for a plain bold "=" character for the exact-match badge (reads more directly as "the same thing"; the genre-only badge's `pricetag` icon was already liked, left untouched) — since Ionicons has no literal equals-sign glyph, `PosterRow.tsx`/`PosterCoverflow.tsx`'s shared `badgeFor` contract (now exported as `PosterBadge` from `PosterRow.tsx`) was widened from icon-only to `{ icon, color } | { char, color }`, with both renderers branching on `"icon" in badge` to draw either an `Ionicons` glyph or a bold `Text` character inside the same badge circle. A compact two-row legend was added under the card itself (badge circle + one-line explanation per row, stacked, sized to stay small relative to the card) spelling out what each badge means, rather than relying on the symbols alone.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed the legend strings and the new `"="`-badge path compiled in, and that the old `checkmark-circle` badge is gone from `MatchSharedFavorites`'s own compiled chunk.

### Backend, same day: Shared Genres' two hard caps removed, and its poster-matching rule made consistent with what the Taste score actually rewards

Two requests, both purely `backend/controllers/matchController.js`, no mobile changes needed since the client already renders however many items come back:

**Caps removed.** `buildMatchInsights`'s `sharedGenres` no longer `.slice(0, 5)`s (the now-unused `MATCH_INSIGHTS_TOP_GENRES` constant removed) — every genre both users have watched anything in comes back, still sorted by combined watch count, heaviest overlap first; the client's own one-at-a-time arrow carousel already handles any count without a crowded chip row. `getSharedGenreContent` no longer `.slice(0, 10)`s per genre either.

**Real, verified mismatch found and fixed**: before touching anything, checked whether the premise behind "should shared *low* ratings count too, not just shared high ones" actually holds — it does. `computeMatchBreakdown`'s `avgRatingSimilarity` (the half of the "Taste"/`collaborative` score that looks at rating values) is `1 - mean(|diff|)/10`, a symmetric distance: two people both rating something 2/10 scores identically to both rating it 9/10. But `getSharedGenreContent` (the actual poster content shown per genre) required both ratings `>= 7` with **no closeness check between them at all** — a 7 and a 10 counted as a match, while two people both rating something a 2 (clearly aligned, just a shared dislike) never showed up anywhere. Fixed to match the score's own philosophy: the `>= 7` floor and its `SHARED_GENRE_CONTENT_MIN_RATING` constant are gone, replaced by `SHARED_GENRE_CONTENT_MAX_RATING_DEVIATION = 2` — both sides just need to be rated within 2 points of each other, on the model's native 1-10 scale, regardless of whether that's a shared high or a shared low. Also added a sort by ascending rating-gap (closest agreement first) per genre, since removing both the floor and the cap means a genre can now return a long, previously-unordered list, and the closest-agreement items are the strongest "you two really line up here" evidence.

Live-verified against real seeded accounts, not just read: `getSwipeQueue` for `Zachary.Macejkovic73330` now returns candidates with up to 19 shared genres (`Peter.Altenwerth29467`, `Nurelski`) — well past the old cap of 5. `getSharedGenreContent` for that same pair returned 15 Drama / 12 Comedy / 11 Action titles (all past the old cap of 10), sorted with `diff: 0` items first, all included items within the new deviation bound. `node --check` clean on the edited controller. (Separately confirmed: the LLM-prompt formatter's own `shared_genres.common_genres` list, used only for the AI-narrative prompt, still caps at 5 independently of `matchInsights.sharedGenres` — a different function, deliberately untouched, not a regression.) Also fixed one stale piece of copy this same change made inaccurate: the Shared Genres empty-state text used to say "...haven't both rated a {{genre}} title highly" — no longer true now that the criterion is closeness, not a high-rating floor — reworded to "...haven't both rated a {{genre}} title similarly."

### New "Variety" card added between Shared Favorites and Social Overlap — the breakdown's diversity score made visible as actual genres

Design discussion first, then build, per the user's own "let's decide the design before implementing" ask: of the 5 weighted breakdown categories (Taste/Favorites/Social/Variety/Activity), only the first 3 had a dedicated detail card; Variety and Activity didn't. Recommended and approved: for Variety specifically, rather than an abstract stat card, show each person's own genre spread as two small horizontal stacked bars (one segment per genre, sized by that person's own watch count in it) — a bar dominated by one or two wide segments reads as "sticks to a few favorites", many similarly-sized segments reads as "explores widely", which is literally what the diversity score's entropy math measures, just shown instead of computed into a number. Activity was scoped out of this round (needs new backend-exposed "recently watched together" data, a bigger lift than Variety's).

**Backend** (`matchController.js`): `computeMatchBreakdown` already has each user's *full, unfiltered* CineGraph (`myGraph`/`targetGraph`) in scope — the same one `calculateDiversityScoreInMemory` itself uses (deliberately not the request's genre-filtered `g1`/`g2`: an active genre filter should narrow Taste/Favorites, but "how wide-ranging are your tastes overall" would be a contradiction in terms if it only looked at whatever genre was just filtered down to). Added a `genreDistribution(graph)` helper (`{genre, count}[]`, sorted by count descending, zero-count genres dropped) and a new `matchInsights.genreDiversity: { mine, theirs }` field built from it — no new query, this data was already computed in-memory for the score itself.

**Mobile**: new `MatchGenreCount`/`MatchGenreDiversity` types (`types/index.ts`), new `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` — two labeled stacked bars ("You" / the candidate's username) built with `flex: share` segments (no manual width-percent math), colored via the same `genreColor`/`hexLuminance` helpers already used elsewhere in this feature so genre colors read as one consistent system across cards. Capped at the top 6 genres (by combined watch count across both people) getting their own color + one shared legend below both bars — the rest of each person's real spread still counts toward their own bar's proportions, just collapsed into a single neutral "Other" segment, since a legend for up to 19 genres wouldn't fit under a card. The card's own description text is pulled from `matchCategoryMeta.ts`'s existing `diversity` copy (not duplicated), so the radar chart's "Variety" axis and this new card describe it identically. Wired into `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx`'s card list as `key: "variety"`, pushed between `"favorites"` and `"social"`, only rendered when either side has any genre data.

Verified: `node --check` clean on the backend controller; live-fetched `getSwipeQueue` confirmed `matchInsights.genreDiversity.mine`/`.theirs` return real per-genre counts (19 genres each for the `Zachary`/`Peter` test pair). `npx tsc --noEmit` clean on mobile; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` and the new `"variety"` card key both compiled in. Not yet visually screenshotted on-device (no simulator/Expo Go session available in this environment) — the data flow and compilation are verified, the actual on-screen bar/legend layout has not been eyeballed live yet.

### Immediate follow-up, same day: Variety redesigned from stacked bars to two bubble-packed circles, per direct "this isn't clear from a customer's eyes" feedback

Direct feedback that the stacked-bar version above wasn't self-explanatory to a first-time viewer. Discussed a Venn-diagram alternative the user proposed themselves (two overlapping empty circles, genre dots placed inside) — and, per their own follow-up observation, talked through why literal overlap is the wrong metaphor here: two overlapping circles visually mean "shared between the two", which is already the Shared Genres card's own job, and would bury Variety's actual signal (how concentrated vs. spread ONE person's own taste is) under a shared/unshared reading Variety doesn't measure at all. Landed on and built: two SEPARATE (non-overlapping), outlined, empty circles — one per person — each packed with a bubble per genre, sized by that person's own watch count in it. One bubble swallowing the circle reads as "sticks to a few favorites"; a scatter of similarly-sized bubbles reads as "explores widely" — same entropy math as before, now shown spatially instead of as bar-segment widths.

`MatchVarietyBars.tsx` replaced outright by new `MatchVarietyBubbles.tsx` (old file deleted, import/usage in `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx` updated) — the data contract (`genreDiversity`, `targetUsername`) is unchanged, only the visual. Circle packing is hand-rolled (no bubble-chart/d3-pack dependency exists for RN here, and item count is always small — at most 6 legend genres + 1 "Other" bucket) via an outward Archimedean-spiral search: place the largest bubble at the circle's center, then for each smaller one walk an expanding spiral until a position is found that overlaps nothing already placed and stays inside the circle.

**Real bug caught before it ever reached device, via a standalone geometry simulation (not a guess)**: the first radius formula (`min + (max-min)*sqrt(value/ownMax)`, independent of item count) let every bubble approach the same near-maximum radius whenever a person's genres were evenly spread across many genres — simulating it directly (outside the app, plain Node) showed 7-, 21-, and even a structural 1-overlap-guaranteed case for as few as *two* equal-value genres, because a single circle's own area budget was being ignored: several same-size, near-max-radius bubbles can't geometrically fit in a fixed container regardless of how good the placement search is. Fixed by switching to an **area-conserving** formula — each bubble's *area* (not radius) is `PACK_FILL_RATIO` (0.2) of the container's own area, scaled by that genre's share of the person's total — so the combined area of all of one person's bubbles stays within a fixed budget no matter how many genres they have, which any placement search can then actually satisfy. Re-verified via the same standalone simulation across hand-picked edge cases (a single genre, two equal genres, one dominant + many tiny, seven equal genres) and 500 randomized item-count/value combinations: zero overlaps, zero bubbles rendered outside their circle, in every run.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed `MatchVarietyBubbles.tsx` compiled in (with `PACK_FILL_RATIO`) and the old `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` fully gone from the bundle. The packing geometry itself was verified via the standalone Node simulation described above, not by reading the on-device layout — still not visually screenshotted (no simulator/Expo Go session available in this environment).

### Immediate follow-up, same day: bubbles didn't land either — back to bars, this time uncapped with no "Other", genres widest-to-narrowest, avatars instead of text labels

Direct feedback that the bubble version wasn't it either — back to the bar design, with concrete changes: no more "Other" bucket, both bars always the card's own full width regardless of how much either person has watched, genre segments ordered widest-to-narrowest within each bar (not the shared bubble-legend's global ranking), no numeric/percentage anywhere ("understood from the bar sizes themselves"), each genre keeps one consistent color, and a small round avatar — sized to the bar's own height, not a text label — sitting at the start of each bar.

Dropping the "Other" bucket turned out to fall out naturally once every genre gets its own segment with no cap at all: since each segment's width is `flex: count` and nothing is excluded, the segments always sum to the full bar by construction — there's no leftover to bucket into an "Other" catch-all in the first place, unlike the earlier capped-at-6 version. `MatchVarietyBubbles.tsx` deleted; `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` rebuilt from scratch (not restored from its own git history, since the ask has real differences from that first bar version too — that one still capped at 6 genres + "Other" + a shared legend; this one has none of those). Colors are still assigned from one shared map built across the *union* of both people's genres (so a genre that appears in both bars is the same color in each — the only cross-bar reference point now that there's no legend spelling out names), but each bar's own segment *order* is independent, sorted by that person's own count — the two bars can (and often will) order their widest-to-narrowest segments differently, since they reflect two different people's own distributions. Avatars reuse the existing shared `UserAvatar` component (same one `MatchTierRow` already uses for this exact "You" + candidate pairing), at `size={22}` to match `BAR_HEIGHT`, left tappable to the profile (not `disabled`) — consistent with how `MatchTierRow`'s own avatars in the same panel already behave.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed the new `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` (with `ROW_GAP`/avatar wiring) compiled in and every trace of the bubble version (`MatchVarietyBubbles.tsx`, `PACK_FILL_RATIO`) is gone. Still not visually screenshotted on-device.

### Real backend bug found while chasing "the bars still look equal-width": CineGraph's `count` field was never incrementing on live ratings, silently affecting the actual Taste and Diversity scores too, not just this new card

User reported the bars still looked evenly split even with this design's real `flex: count` proportional segments — a legitimate thing to check, not dismissed as "must be the data." Read `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` again first to rule out a code bug (none — `flex: seg.share` where `share = g.count` is genuinely proportional, confirmed by re-reading the exact lines). Then checked the actual data live rather than guessing: `Nurelski`'s (a real account, 1013 real `Rating` documents queried directly from MongoDB) `matchInsights.genreDiversity` showed `count: 1` for every single one of their 19 movie genres — impossible to be a coincidence at that rating volume.

Root cause, found by tracing where the CineGraph field actually gets written: `ratingController.js`'s `updateCineGraph` (the function that runs on every live rating create/update through the normal app flow) had a real, previously-diagnosed bug — its incremental-average branch updated `ratedCount`/`avgRating` but never `count`, the field `computeMatchBreakdown`'s own `g1`/`g2` (Taste's genre-overlap half) and `calculateGenreEntropy` (the *entire* Diversity/"Variety" score, not just this new card) both actually read. This diagnosis and its fix already existed in the working tree (staged, uncommitted — likely from an earlier, now-summarized part of this same session) but had never been committed. Confirmed the exact fix (`count: node.count + 1` added alongside the existing `ratedCount`/`avgRating` updates) was correct and scoped to only this bug, then committed it (`ef040e2`) at the user's explicit choice, after presenting the tradeoffs: commit-only (fixes it going forward, existing accounts' historical counts stay frozen at whatever they were) vs. also backfilling every existing user's CineGraph from their real Rating history (fixes existing accounts immediately, larger/riskier change since it can shift real users' live match percentages) vs. doing nothing this round. User picked commit-only.

**Practical consequence for testing this card**: seeded/demo accounts (`Zachary.Macejkovic73330`, `Nurelski`, etc.) will keep showing flat, equal-width bars — their historical `count` values are frozen from before this fix and weren't backfilled. A genuinely skewed bar (e.g., an account that's rated many titles in one genre and few in another) will only show up for ratings added *from now on* through the live app, or for an account whose CineGraph gets rebuilt by whatever already-correct path bulk import/rebuild scripts use. This is a real, understood limitation to flag when next testing this card, not a residual bug in `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` itself.

### Fourth design for this card: bars dropped too — two of the Sync page's own genre-ring donuts, side by side, no filter chips

Direct realization from the user: rather than inventing yet another bespoke visualization, reuse the exact ring the user already sees and understands on the Sync/filter page (`CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`) — two of those donuts side by side, one per person, each with that person's own avatar at the center, but with the surrounding filter-chip buttons stripped out entirely ("sadece graphlar olacak etrafındaki butonlar değil").

Neither `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx` (the Sync page's own filter picker) nor `CineGraphDonut.tsx` (Profile's version, with tap-to-see-detail chips) could be reused directly — both are ~500-line files built inseparably around their own chip layout math (fixed genre zone tables, per-row nudges, tap-to-select state), and the user explicitly wants none of that here, only the ring and a center avatar. Built a third, much smaller, standalone copy instead: new `MatchVarietyRings.tsx`, a `GenreRing` sub-component rendering just the ring (one full circle per genre, only a count-proportional arc visible via `strokeDasharray`/`strokeDashoffset`, exactly the same SVG technique as the other two files) plus a center `UserAvatar` (`disabled`, non-interactive) — no chips, no rotation/loading animation, no selection state. `MatchVarietyBars.tsx` deleted.

**Real width bug caught before it shipped, by recognizing a precedent already documented in this exact file**: the first draft sized the two rings off `useWindowDimensions()`'s raw screen width, doing the padding-chain math (card padding, `cardWidth`, the cloud's own width cap) by hand to estimate the available space — exactly the class of bug `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx`'s own `containerWidth` prop doc comment already describes having happened once before in this same feature (a panel that used to size its cards off the full screen width instead of its real container, pushing content past the visible edge). Caught it on a second read rather than shipping it, and switched to measuring the row's own real layout width via `onLayout` instead — the same fix pattern `PosterCoverflow.tsx`'s `viewportWidth` already uses in this codebase, rather than reimplementing (and risking re-breaking) the padding math independently a third time.

**Real boundary-line bug also caught and fixed before shipping**, via careful comparison against `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s own working boundary math rather than trusting a plausible-looking first draft: the divider-line angles were computed at each slice's *end* (cumulative count *after* adding it) and then `.slice(0, -1)`-trimmed to drop what looked like a redundant final entry — but for N slices arranged around a closed ring, there are exactly N dividers, not N-1 (the line before the first slice and the line after the last one are the same line, at the wrap-around point), so end-of-slice indexing plus trimming the last entry actually drops the *wrong* one — the wrap-around divider between the last and first slice, specifically. Fixed by switching to start-of-slice indexing with no trim, matching `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s own `slices` boundary computation exactly (a divider is pushed *before* each slice's own count is added to the running total, one per slice, all of them drawn).

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed `MatchVarietyRings.tsx` (with `onRowLayout`) compiled in and the bar version (`MatchVarietyBars.tsx`) is fully gone. The boundary-line fix was verified by direct comparison against the already-shipped `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx` math, not by eyeballing the ring on-device — still not visually screenshotted.

### Fifth (and simplest) design for this card: stop computing anything server-side — just fetch each person's already-existing, already-correct CineGraph and reuse Profile's own ring, chip-free

Direct correction from the user, and the right one: don't invent a backend computation for this at all — both people's CineGraph already exists and is already fetched elsewhere in this exact app (Profile's own CineGraph tab, `getCineGraph(userId)` → `CineGraphDonut.tsx`). Fetch that directly, reuse that ring's own drawing technique, just smaller and without its chip buttons — nothing else.

This mattered more than it first looked like, for a reason only found by actually re-checking the data live rather than assuming the previous approach was merely "a worse design": `matchInsights.genreDiversity` (this card's previous data source, `backend/controllers/matchController.js`) was built by reading `me[cineKey]`/`target[cineKey]` — the same **stale, cached CineGraph field on the User document** whose live-rating sync bug was found and fixed two rounds ago (see the "CineGraph count field" entry above). `getUserCineGraph` (`backend/controllers/userController.js`, what `getCineGraph` on mobile calls) turns out to be a completely different, **already-correct code path** — it recomputes genre counts and average ratings live, on every request, straight from the user's actual `watchlist` + `Rating` documents, never touching that stale cached field at all. Live-verified head to head: `matchInsights.genreDiversity` (the abandoned approach) showed `count: 1` for every genre for a 1013-rating account; `getCineGraph` for that same account, same moment, returned real varied counts (`Comedy: 425, Drama: 375, Fantasy: 199, Documentary: 26, ...`). So this wasn't just a simpler implementation — it was also the only one of the two that actually worked correctly against real data, on accounts whose historical `count` field the earlier fix didn't (and, by design, wasn't asked to) retroactively repair.

Reverted the now-unnecessary backend addition entirely: `buildMatchInsights`'s `genreDiversity` field, its `genreDistribution` helper, and the `myGraph`/`targetGraph` params threaded into it — all removed from `matchController.js`, back to exactly its prior shape. Removed the matching `MatchGenreCount`/`MatchGenreDiversity` mobile types.

`MatchVarietyRings.tsx` rewritten a second time: `MatchAnalysisPanel.tsx` now passes only `candidate` (no more `genreDiversity` prop — the component fetches for itself), and it calls `getCineGraph` twice on mount/candidate-change (once for the viewer via `useAuth()`, once for `candidate.user._id`), each guarded with the same cancellation-flag pattern this file already uses elsewhere. Its `GenreRing` sub-component is now a much closer, deliberate copy of `CineGraphDonut.tsx`'s own remaining (post-chip-removal) behavior — the same ring-drawing technique, and the same tap-a-slice center-reveal (total item count, or the tapped genre's own count/%/rating) — rather than a from-scratch reimplementation. Two things fall out of removing the chip ring as a direct, unavoidable consequence rather than extra scope: `CineGraphDonut`'s rotate-on-select animation (it only ever existed to spin the tapped slice into alignment with its own chip; with no chip, nothing to align to) and its "Detail" button (which, per a separate finding while reading `ProfileCinegraphsTab.tsx` for this exact task, always navigates to the *viewer's own* profile route regardless of whose CineGraph is open — a real, pre-existing, out-of-scope bug for the "other person's ring" case that this component avoids inheriting simply by not having a Detail button at all). A small caption (`"You"` / the candidate's username) sits under each ring — the minimum needed to tell two side-by-side rings apart, since neither carries an avatar the way `CineMatchGenreRing.tsx`'s own version does.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; `node --check` clean on the reverted backend controller; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed the new `getCineGraph`-based `MatchVarietyRings.tsx` compiled in and every trace of `genreDiversity` is gone from both the backend file and the bundle. Live-verified `GET /api/users/cinegraph-data/:id` directly against three real accounts (self, a candidate, the 1013-rating account) — `isAuthorized: true` and real, varied `movieStats` for all three, confirming both that the endpoint works for arbitrary users (not just "me") and that its data is genuinely correct, not just structurally present.

### Sixth pass on this card: rings made fully passive (avatars instead of tap/reveal), a Shared-Genres-style scrollable genre picker added below, driving a cross-ring gray/highlight and a You-vs-them item-count comparison

Direct follow-up spec, several concrete pieces at once:
- Rings stop being tappable entirely — no slice `onPress`, no per-genre reveal inside the ring itself.
- Each ring's center goes back to an avatar (`UserAvatar`, `disabled`) instead of the item-count text `CineGraphDonut.tsx` normally shows there; the "You"/username caption that used to sit *under* each ring (added two rounds ago, once there was no avatar to identify a ring by) is removed now that the avatar does that job again.
- A new horizontal, scrollable genre-chip picker sits below both rings — visually and mechanically the same shape as this panel's own Shared Genres/Favorites poster rows (gesture-handler `ScrollView` for the same nested-same-axis-scroll reason, a right-edge fade hinting more to scroll) — containing every genre present in *either* person's CineGraph, the full union, uncapped.
- Tapping a chip selects that genre (tapping the same one again deselects, back to the default/idle state where nothing is selected). Selecting a genre dims every *other* slice in *both* rings to gray at once, leaving only the matching slice (if that person has it at all) in its own color — and if one person doesn't have that genre at all, every one of their own slices dims, since none of their slices ever matches the selected genre.
- Below the picker, a two-column "You" / candidate-username detail readout — total item count for each person by default, or (once a genre is selected) that specific genre's item count for each — mirroring the same two-column comparison shape this panel's own Shared Genres/Favorites cards already use, just with a plain item count instead of a star rating.

Implementation notes: the rotate-on-select/"Detail"-button removals from the previous round turned out to be exactly the right call in hindsight — this round's picker-driven selection model has no chip-alignment concept at all (selection lives in a completely separate scrollable row now, not on the ring), so there was nothing left to rotate toward even if the fifth round had kept it. Colors are computed once, in the parent, across the *union* of both people's genres (ranked by combined count, same convention every earlier round of this card has used) and threaded down as a shared `colorByGenre` map to both rings and the picker, rather than each ring computing its own local palette — the only way a genre can consistently mean "this exact color" everywhere it appears. `genreRatings` (fetched by `getCineGraph` alongside `movieStats`/`seriesStats`) is no longer used anywhere in this card now that the ring's own per-genre rating display is gone — left unused rather than special-cased out of the fetch, since `getCineGraph` returns both together in one call regardless.

Live-verified the "genre missing from one side → that whole ring grays out" case is real and testable with the existing `Zachary`/`Peter` pair, not just theoretically possible: `Peter.Altenwerth29467` has `Family` and `Animation` in their movie CineGraph that `Zachary.Macejkovic73330` has zero of.

Verified: `npx tsc --noEmit` clean; fresh Metro bundle fetch confirmed the new `GenrePicker`/`colorByGenre`/selection logic compiled in and the old per-ring tap-reveal/rating-display code is gone. Still not visually screenshotted on-device.

### Seventh pass: tap-to-select replaced with PosterCoverflow's own center-focus auto-select, headers restyled to match Shared Genres exactly, unit label swapped from "items" to movies/series

Direct follow-up: the tap-based `GenrePicker` chip row from the previous round is gone, replaced with `GenreCoverflow` — mechanically the exact same center-focus coverflow `PosterCoverflow.tsx` already uses for Shared Genres/Favorites (same `scrollX`-listener/pitch-rounding technique deciding which item is "focused," same `AnimatedGHScrollView` wrapping for the same nested-same-axis-scroll reason, same mount-effect auto-focusing index 0), just rendering genre pills instead of poster images — scrolling brings a genre chip to the center and that's what gets selected, no tap involved. Since a coverflow always has *some* real item centered (index 0 at rest, same as Shared Genres' own carousel), the earlier "nothing selected by default" idle state from two rounds ago is superseded here: `selectedGenre` is never null once data loads, so the detail readout below always shows a specific genre's numbers, never an ambiguous "totals across everything" state.
